title: Douro
description: Terraced schist slopes above a river: the home of Port and of Portugal's great dry reds.
L: A river valley carved in schist

The Douro river runs west from Spain to Porto and the Atlantic. Its wine region, in northern Portugal, starts about 100 km inland, behind the Marão mountains, which block Atlantic rain. Vineyards line the steep valley sides and tributaries. It's divided into three sub-regions: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.

The Marão creates a rain shadow, so the Douro grows hotter and drier from west to east. Baixo Corgo, in the west, gets about 900 mm of rain; the Douro Superior, near Spain, about 400 mm. Summers often reach 40 degrees. Schist soil, which splits vertically, lets roots dig deep for water.
What protects the Douro from Atlantic rain?
The Marão casts a rain shadow over the valley.

In 1756, the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro and created a company to control Port's quality and trade, making it one of the world's first legally defined wine regions. Stone markers, marcos, set the boundaries. In 2001, the Alto Douro Wine Region became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Yes, by the Marquis of Pombal.
The Douro lies behind the Marão, in three sub-regions
It gets hotter and drier towards Spain
It was demarcated in 1756 and is a UNESCO site

The Douro allows over 100 grapes, but five are recommended for quality. Touriga Nacional: floral, dark, structured. Touriga Franca, the most planted: perfumed, elegant. Tinta Roriz, Tempranillo: red fruit and body. Tinta Barroca: soft, sweet fruit, early ripening. Tinto Cão: acidity and finesse, low yields.

Many old Douro vineyards are field blends, vinhas velhas, with dozens of grapes planted together, often over 80 years old. They're picked and fermented together, giving complexity. Whites, from Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio and Códega do Larinho, grow at higher, cooler sites and make dry whites and white Port.
Match each grape to its role.
Douro blends draw on many natives.
Vinhas velhas, old vines, on a Douro label often means a field blend of many grapes, a living record of how the region was planted.
Which is the Douro's most planted grape?
Touriga Franca covers the most area.
Five recommended reds lead, from Touriga Nacional to Tinto Cão
Touriga Franca is the most planted

Douro soils are mostly schist, a layered rock that splits vertically. Roots follow the cracks deep, sometimes 10 metres or more, to find water in dry summers. Schist also stores heat. Granite appears at the edges, but the best Port vineyards are on schist; the boundary between schist and granite roughly marks the region.

To plant on slopes up to 60 degrees, people built terraces by hand. Old terraces, socalcos, have dry-stone walls and narrow ledges. From the 1970s, patamares, wider terraces without walls, allowed some machines. Vinha ao alto, vertical planting up the slope, is used where it's less steep. All are labour-intensive.
Match each term to its meaning.
The Douro's landscape is built by hand.

Douro vineyards for Port are classified from A to F, based on factors like altitude, yield, soil, slope, exposure and vine age. A and B vineyards receive the most authorisation to make Port, the beneficio, and the highest grape prices. Cima Corgo has the highest share of top-graded vineyards.
Why does schist suit the Douro?
Roots follow its vertical cracks to find water
Schist lets roots dig deep for water
Socalcos, patamares and vinha ao alto shape the slopes
Vineyards are graded A to F for Port

Port grapes are crushed, traditionally by foot in stone tanks, lagares, now often by machine or robotic pistons. After two or three days of fermentation, at about 6 to 9% alcohol, aguardente, grape spirit at about 77%, is added, stopping fermentation. The result: about 19 to 22% alcohol and 90 to 110 g/l of sugar. Wine ages in Vila Nova de Gaia or the Douro.

Ruby styles age briefly in large vats, keeping dark colour and fresh fruit: Ruby, Reserve, Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, a single year bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood, and Vintage. Tawny styles age in small casks, pipes, where oxygen gives nutty, caramel notes: Tawny, Reserve Tawny, aged tawnies with 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, and Colheita, a single-vintage tawny.
Vats for ruby; casks for tawny
Match each Port to its ageing.
How Port ages defines its style.

Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years, declared by each house, about three times a decade. It's bottled after two to three years and ages for decades in bottle, throwing a sediment. Single quinta Vintages come from one estate in good, undeclared years. White and rosé Ports add lighter styles.
Declared about three times a decade
Aged tawny is cask-aged, a tawny style.
Port is fortified with aguardente mid-fermentation
Ruby styles age in vats or bottle; tawnies in casks
Vintage Port is declared in exceptional years
The new face of the Douro

For centuries, most Douro grapes went into Port. Barca Velha, first made in 1952 by Fernando Nicolau de Almeida at Ferreira, showed the Douro could make great dry reds. From the 1990s, producers like Niepoort, Quinta do Crasto and Quinta do Vale Meão built the modern dry Douro. Today dry wines rival Port in volume.

Dry Douro reds are dark and structured, with black fruit, violet, rockrose and schist minerality, often blends of Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz. Top wines age in French oak and can age 15 to 20 years. Higher, cooler sites give fresher styles. Douro whites, from Rabigato and Viosinho, are crisp and mineral.
Which wine showed in 1952 that the Douro could make great dry reds?
Some Douro producers make both Port and dry wine from the same quinta, a chance to taste how fortification changes the same fruit.
Dry wines now rival Port in volume in the Douro.
Yes. Dry Douro DOC wines have grown greatly since the 1990s.
Barca Velha, 1952, began the dry Douro tradition
Dry reds are dark, floral and structured
Douro whites from high sites are crisp and mineral
Reading the Douro and eating with it

Dry wines are labelled Douro DOC; fortified wines Porto DOC. Port labels show the style: Ruby, Tawny, LBV, Vintage, Colheita, or an age like 20 Years Old. Quinta means estate. The IVDP, the Douro and Port institute, seals each bottle. Vinhas velhas means old vines.

Dry Douro reds suit roast kid, lamb, bacalhau with roasted potatoes, and game. Ruby and Vintage Port suit Stilton and dark chocolate. Tawny suits crème brûlée, nuts, caramel desserts and Portuguese pastries like pastéis de nata. White Port with tonic is Porto's aperitif. Serve tawny slightly cool.
Stilton with Vintage; nuts with tawny
Porto tónico, white Port and tonic.

Serve ruby and Vintage Port at about 16 degrees, tawnies at 10 to 14, white Port chilled. Decant Vintage Port and unfiltered LBV for sediment. Opened tawnies last weeks; Vintage Port is best within a day or two.
Douro DOC is dry; Porto DOC is fortified
Dry reds suit lamb; Vintage Port suits Stilton
Decant Vintage Port; tawnies keep after opening
